newsitem.title: USA: Kansas corn growers advised to test for aflatoxin.
newsitem.headline: Kansas corn growers advised to test for aflatoxin.

text.p: Kansas corn producers should consider testing their 1996 crop for aflatoxin and other mycotoxins, a Kansas State University Extension specialist said.
"We have diagnosed several corn samples with ear molds. Other labs are reporting this, too," said Doug Jardine, KSU Etension plant pathologist.

Jardine's advisory came a day after an official at the Kansas Department of Agriculture told Reuters that a shipment of milk from a Kansas dairy was destroyed after it was found to contain aflatoxin levels that exceeded federal limits.
Jardine said in a news release mailed Wednesday that at least four kinds of ear mold were present in corn samples received at the Plant Disease Diagnostic Center.
"We have found Aspergillus ear rot, which causes aflatoxin, and Fusarium, Gibberella and Diplodia ear rot," Jardine said.

Kansas Department of Agriculture's Grain Inspection Service laboratory in Topeka also found isolated cases of aflatoxin in new-crop corn samples and last week issued an aflatoxin alert advising corn producers to test their grain.

Aflatoxin is a carcinogenic substance that occurs naturally in some grain. For that reason, the Food and Drug places strict limits on allowable amounts that can be detected in milk and in grain for human or animal feed.

Jardine said livestock that are fed Giberella-infected corn often refuse feed, vomit or show signs of estrogenic syndrome. Diplodia causes grayish brown, shrunken ears and light test weights, he said. It is not toxic, but it can cause dockage due to poor grain quality.
Jardine said most of the samples testing positive for aflatoxin came from northeast Kansas terminal elevators and rated positive at 30 to 95 parts per billion (ppb).
Under FDA rules, grain containing more than 20 ppb of aflatoxin may not be used for human consumption or as feed for immature animals, poultry or dairy animals.
Grain testing between 20 and 100 ppb can be used as feed for breeding cattle, swine and mature poultry.

Grain testing at 100 to 200 ppb is suitable for finishing swine over 100 pounds or beef cattle. Levels between 200 and 300 ppb limit grain use to finishing beef cattle only. Grain testing higher than 300 ppb cannot be used as feed unless it is cleaned, ammoniated or diluted (blended) with clean grain.
